title: Daniel Kerchner’s personal academic website
text:
Quarto website (no executable code cells) published to https://kerchner.github.io. Source of truth for content is Dan’s CV PDF (kept at repo root, untracked).



_quarto.yml — site config: navbar, footer, cosmo base theme + styles/theme.scss (light) and styles/theme-dark.scss (dark)
index.qmd — trestles-style about page (headshot, bio, education, highlights)
experience.qmd, research.qmd, teaching.qmd, publications.qmd, presentations.qmd — content pages
assets/ — kerchner-cv.pdf and DanHeadshot.jpg (stable filenames; linked from multiple pages)





Publications/presentations are hand-authored markdown lists (not Quarto listings or BibTeX). Dan’s name bolded (**Kerchner D.**), DOIs linked as https://doi.org/<doi>, reverse-chronological within sections.
Never link URL shorteners (bit.ly/tinyurl) — resolve and link the canonical destination; use archive.org if the original is dead.
When updating the CV, overwrite assets/kerchner-cv.pdf in place — do not add dated filenames; the link URL must stay stable.
Contact email is kerchner@gwu.edu (not kerchner@email.gwu.edu).
Keep the two SCSS themes’ typography identical; only colors differ between light and dark.





Source lives on main; the rendered site is force-pushed to gh-pages by Quarto. GitHub Pages serves the gh-pages branch (do not switch it back to main — that serves raw .qmd files).
To deploy: commit changes to main (publish requires a clean working tree), then quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt.
Preview locally with quarto preview; _site/ and .quarto/ are generated and git-ignored.
Dan’s pre-2021 Jekyll site lives in the separate kerchner-old-personal-site repo — unrelated to this one.

title: Professional Experience
text:
May 2013 – Present
Senior Software Developer and Librarian, GW Libraries
Developing open-source web applications and infrastructure supporting digital preservation and archiving, web development, catalog integration, and library information technology. Sharing expertise with students, researchers, and faculty by providing consultations and teaching workshops in Python, R, and related topics focused on data skills. Projects include:

Open Access Analytics — Building a data pipeline and executive-level dashboard to track compliance with GW’s new Open Access Policy across faculty-authored scholarly publications.
GW ScholarSpace — Primary software developer of GWU’s institutional open-access scholarship repository, built with Hyrax, Ruby on Rails, and other technologies.
The ISIS Files — Primary software developer for a Hyrax-based public repository of specialized artifacts, in collaboration with the GW Program on Extremism.
Social Feed Manager — Software developer of this GWU-built tool that helps researchers build collections of social media data from Twitter and other platforms. Built with Python, Django, PostgreSQL, Docker, APScheduler, RabbitMQ, and other technologies. Worked with numerous researchers in the GWU community to build collections of interest.

Adjunct Instructor, Milken Institute School of Public Health
Co-creator and co-instructor of a new 1-credit course, Introduction to R Programming in Public Health and Biomedical Research (PUBH 6899 / PUBH 6851), offered through the Milken Institute School of Public Health Summer Institute. Delivered online in Summer 2020 and Summer 2021.

title: Daniel Kerchner
text:
I am a Data Scientist, Software Developer, Bioinformatician, and Instructor with over 20 years of software development and project management experience, as well as advanced biostatistics skills.
I am currently a PhD student in Health Data Science – Bioinformatics at George Washington University, with research interests in applying artificial intelligence to the analysis of genomic, metabolomic, microbiome, and other omics data. In my doctoral research, I am applying novel genomic language models (gLMs) to improve omics characterization over traditional, search-based techniques.
For the past eight years, I have been a sought-after health data science consultant and instructor both within and beyond GW. As an expert R and Python programmer, I practice and advocate for best practices in collaborative, open, and reproducible research — and I teach other researchers the fundamental data and computational skills they need to grow and succeed in their research.
